title: 絵師一家、知行の宣旨に喜ぶ
gendaibun: 朝廷から知行を与える宣旨を受け、絵師は身に余る光栄と喜んだ。家に帰ると妻子や眷属が集まり、まだ納めていない年貢の書類まで作り始めて大はしゃぎし、祝宴の酒に酔った使者は縁から転んで酒をこぼしたという。
kobun: 朝恩（ちょうおん）なれば忝（かたじ）けなく、悦事（よろこぶこと）限りなし。此由（このよし）家に帰りて語りければ、妻子眷属（さいしけんぞく）ども走り集ひて、いまだ未倒の土貢（どこう）の納所（なっしょ）を求め認（したため）むる有様、笑ひ罵る声々、天地を響かして、物音も聞こえ侍らずぞありし。然（き）る程に、老母をはじめとして、疎（うと）からぬ輩と賀酒（がのさけ）を飲みけるが、早や酔（え）いぬれば、乱舞一声に及ぶままに、次第に飲み叱りつつ、酒又取り寄せけるが、使も酔いぬれば、縁の破れに足を入て倒れければ、酒もこぼしぬ。使（つかい）しかねて水を入加へて出だしたりけれども、皆酔いぬる心地には、善悪を弁（わきま）へずして、其日は朝（あした）より飲み暮らし侍りけるとかや。
desc: 絵師草紙は、鎌倉時代の絵師の貧しい境遇を、みずからの体験にもとづいて描いたといわれる絵巻です。この段では、絵師が領地（知行）を与えられたという朝廷の宣旨を受けて、一家で祝杯をあげる喜びの場面が描かれます。しかし、この「喜び」は次の段で「ぬか喜び」だったことが明かされます。詞書は、酔った使いが酒をこぼすなどの滑稽な細部をユーモラスに描き、喜びの絶頂とその反転を予感させます。鎌倉時代の絵師の身分や暮らしを伝える貴重な資料です。
gendaibunen: Granted a fief by imperial decree, the painter felt overwhelmed with honor and joy. At home his wife, children, and dependents gathered, even drafting receipts for unpaid land tax in high spirits; the messenger, drunk on celebratory sake, tripped on the broken veranda and spilled the wine.
kobunen: Because it was imperial favor, he felt humbly grateful, and his joy knew no bounds. When he returned home and told them, his wife, children, and dependents came running; as they set about drafting receipts for land tax not yet paid, laughter and jeering shook heaven and earth so that no other sound could be heard. Meanwhile his aged mother and those close to him drank congratulatory sake; once tipsy they broke into song and dance, kept drinking and scolding in turn, and sent for more wine. The messenger too grew drunk, caught his foot in a broken spot on the veranda, fell, and spilled the sake. Though he had earlier mixed in water before serving it, all were too drunk to tell good from bad, and that day they drank from morning on, it is said.
descen: The Eshi Sōshi is a scroll thought to depict the poverty of a Kamakura-period painter, drawn from experience. Here the artist and his household celebrate receiving an imperial decree granting him a fief. The joy, however, is revealed in the next scene to be hollow. The caption humorously describes the tipsy messenger spilling sake, foreshadowing the reversal of fortune. The scroll is a rare record of the status and daily life of painters in medieval Japan.
titleen: The artist's family rejoices at the grant of a fief

title: ぬか喜びの宣旨の内容
gendaibun: 翌日内地へ使いを出すと、戻った文には年貢の取れない土地だとだけ書かれていた。家の煙は絶え、庭に人の気配もなく、従う者も散り、残ったのは子を思う老母と夫を慕う妻の悲しみばかりだった。
kobun: 次日（つぎのひ）は急ぎ人拵（こしら）へつつ、田舎へ下遣（くだしつか）はしぬ。然る程に雲煙（うんえん）を凌ぐ海路も、月日過ぐれば、心許ながりつる。雁（かり）の使も帰り来り、先（まず）嬉しくて文（ふみ）を開き見るに、所の有様と覚しくて、土民の武威を高ずる次第、先使（せんし）が取りて年貢のなき事ばかりを書きてこの外は何事も見えざりければ、大方（おおかた）正躰（体）なきに、いよいよ煙絶え行く家の有様、人の跡なき庭の景色、何に命のかかるべきなれば、従類も散り行きて自（おのずか）ら留まる者は、子を思ふ老母の悲しみに惑へる。夫を慕ふ賎婦（せんぷ）の別れを嘆くなどなれば、皆飢を忍び、貧しきを忘て、残ゐ（のこり）たり。この輩（ともがら）を見るに、眼も暮るる心の内、ただ推し量られたり。
desc: 使者が持ち帰った文書には、与えられた土地の実情——年貢がまったく納められない荒れ地であること——だけが記されており、絵師の喜びが無意味だったことが明かされます。煙の絶えた家、人の気配のない庭、子を想う老母の悲しみ、夫を慕う妻の別れの嘆きが、詞書に切々と綴られます。この段は、絵師の絶望を、具体的な生活の光景に落とし込んで描きます。形式どおりの「朝恩」の有難さと、現実の生活の厳しさの落差が、絵巻全体の主題です。
gendaibunen: The next day a messenger was sent to the countryside; the letter that returned said only that the land yielded no annual tribute. Cooking smoke faded from the house, the garden showed no visitors' tracks, dependents drifted away, and those who remained were an old mother grieving for her child and a wife mourning her husband's parting.
kobunen: The next day they hurriedly prepared someone and sent him down to the countryside. Time passed on the cloud-wrapped sea road, and anxiety grew. When the wild-goose messenger returned, they opened the letter with joy—yet it seemed only to describe local conditions, how the peasantry flaunted their force, and that the first envoy had written solely of the absence of annual tribute, with nothing else to be seen. With nothing solid to rely on, the house whose smoke dwindled further, the garden empty of footprints, offered no hold for life; retainers scattered, and those who stayed of their own accord were an old mother lost in grief for her child, or a humble wife sighing over parting from her husband—all enduring hunger and forgetting poverty. Seeing such people, one's eyes grow dim; the anguish within can only be imagined.
descen: The letter the messenger brings back reveals the truth: the granted land is a wasteland that yields no annual tribute at all. The caption poignantly describes a house whose smoke has ceased, an empty garden, a mother weeping for her son, and a wife lamenting her husband's departure. The scene translates the painter's despair into concrete images of daily life. The gap between the formality of imperial favor and the harshness of real life is the central theme of the scroll.
titleen: The hollow joy of the imperial decree

title: 絵師の愁訴①
gendaibun: 絵師は都へ馳せ戻り、絵の奉行をしている上卿の弟のもとに愁訴した。頼れるのは御所のあわれみだけ、私領の知行もなく、家には古い絵本と旧記ばかりで、顔淵の一箪の食・原憲の百結の衣のような貧しさだと訴えた。
kobun: て馳帰りけるが、折節（おりふし）絵の事ども奉行し給（たまい）て、便よく侍りければ、当寺の上卿（しょうけい）の弟（だい）に参りて、「御所様の御哀憐の外は、頼む方なき身の有様を申入ける事どもは、朝恩も侍らず。又、本自（もとより）私の領とて、針を立つる所も知行（ちぎょう）なし。只、古絵本、旧記などをぞ家に伝え侍る。されば明け暮れ顔子一箪（がんしいったん）の食（し）忍び難く、原生百結（げんせいひゃっけつ）の衣恥ずるに足りぬべし。
desc: 絵師は、知行の地が遠方の荒れ地だったため、嘆願のために上洛します。詞書では、古絵本や旧記しか家に伝えるものがない貧しさが述べられ、『顔子一箪の食』『原生百結の衣』といった中国の故事を引いて、みすぼらしい暮らしを表現します。鎌倉時代の絵師は、今日の芸術家とは異なり、注文主に奉公する職人であり、その経済基盤は不安定でした。このような身の上を訴える「申文」をしたため、権力者に直訴する文化があったことを、この絵巻は伝えています。
gendaibunen: The painter raced back to the capital and petitioned the younger brother of a senior courtier then overseeing painting affairs. He said he had only His Lordship's pity to rely on, held no private fief at all, and at home possessed little but old picture books and records—enduring a poverty like Yan Hui's single bamboo bowl and Yuan Xian's hundred-patched coat.
kobunen: He rode back in haste; just then painting matters were being administered, which proved convenient, so he went to the younger brother of the temple's senior courtier and declared: "Apart from His Lordship's compassion, I have no one to rely on; I have received no imperial favor. Nor do I originally hold any private domain—not even land the size of a needle—as a fief. I only keep old picture books and old records at home. Thus from dawn to dusk I can hardly endure food like Yan Hui's single bamboo bowl, and ought to be ashamed of a coat like Yuan Xian's hundred patches."
descen: The painter travels to the capital to plead his case, having discovered that his fief is a remote wasteland. The caption tells of a household that owns nothing but old picture books and documents, citing Chinese sayings—Gan Hui's single bamboo bowl and the hundred-patched coat—to convey his shabby poverty. Unlike artists today, Kamakura-period painters were craftsmen in service to their patrons, with fragile livelihoods. The scroll documents the culture of submitting written petitions and appealing directly to those in power.

title: 絵師の愁訴②
gendaibun: 少年のころから絵の稽古と奉公を重ねてきた身が、せっかくの朝恩を理由なく取り上げられれば都に跡も留めがたく、一流の滅亡になると涙ながらに訴えた。上卿が奏すると、もとの伊州の地を返すとの勅答があったが、絵師はあまりに遠いと重ねて願い出た。
kobun: この思ひ、少年の昔より強仕（きょうし）の今に及ぶまで、寝ても覚めても休む事なし。然れども稽古日を重ね、奉公年を経ぬる上、旧院他ニ異に、召仕侍りしかば、君も如何でか捨てさせ給ふべきに、適（たまたま）の　朝恩、故なく召されぬる事、面目を失うのみにあらず。且（かつ）は宮古（都）に跡を留め難く侍り。させる罪なき身の沈果（しずみは）てなば、既に一流の威（滅）亡となりなんこそ、不便なれ」と、忠実（まめ）やかに悲涙を流しつつ申しければ、上卿急ぎ　奏給ける。　勅答には、哀れみ思し召されけるにや、本の伊州を還給（かえしたまう）べき申うけ給（承）るこそ、先畏（まずかしこまり）覚えしが、其時重ねて申入けるは、「此所あまりに遥かなる上、又興行の沙汰も、身の上なくては、道行き難き間、当時、此地に命を懸けて奉公し難く侍り。
desc: 絵師は、少年の頃から絵の稽古を重ね、長く奉公してきた身の上を訴えます。詞書には、朝廷から与えられた「朝恩」を失えば、一家の家業が滅んでしまうという悲愴な思いが綴られます。上卿（しょうけい）に泣いて訴える姿は、絵巻の中で最も劇的な場面の一つです。結果、朝廷は哀れみ、もとの伊州（いしゅう）の地を返すことを約束しますが、絵師はそれが遠すぎるとして、再び陳情します。貴族に直接文を上げるという、当時の身分社会の現実がうかがえます。
gendaibunen: In tears he pleaded that, having trained and served since boyhood, to lose the imperial favor without cause would leave him no foothold in the capital and destroy his entire school of painting. When the senior courtier reported this, an imperial reply promised to restore his former land in Ishu—but the painter petitioned again, saying the place was too far away.
kobunen: "This resolve—from my boyhood to my present prime—never rests, waking or sleeping. Yet though I piled up days of practice and years of service, and the former retired emperor treated me differently and employed me, how could my lord cast me aside? To have that occasional imperial favor revoked without cause is not only a loss of face; it also makes it hard to keep a foothold in the capital. If an innocent man sinks completely, an entire lineage of our craft will perish—how pitiful!" So he pleaded, faithfully shedding tears of grief; the senior courtier hurriedly reported it. In the imperial reply, perhaps from pity, he was told his original land of Ishu would be restored—at first he felt awed—but then he petitioned again: "That place is far too remote, and without means to develop it, travel is hard; at present I can hardly stake my life on serving there."
descen: The painter pleads that he has trained in painting since boyhood and served faithfully for years. The caption conveys his despair that losing the imperial favor would destroy his family's craft. His tearful appeal to the chief minister is one of the most dramatic moments in the scroll. The court, moved to pity, promises to return his original land of Ishu—but the painter, finding it too distant, petitions again. The scene reveals the realities of petitioning the nobility in the status-bound society of the age.

title: 絵師の愁訴③
gendaibun: 代わりに都に近い小さな小屋を願ったが返事は延び、春半ばになっても決まらず、絵師は盛者必衰を悟って妻子への執着を断ち、子を真言修行の霊場へ遣わした。年が明けてもなお、みずからの道の真の有様を後世に著して残したいと記して愁訴は結ばれる。
kobun: 同じくば、今少し近き小屋に立替て下されなんや」とて、さもありぬべき所々、数多（あまた）記して参らせければ、御案（ごあん）あるべしとばかりうけ給はりて、過ぎにし秋の末つ方より、春も既に半ばになりぬるにや、愁（うれい）の涙も猶色添ふ心地すれば、沈み果てぬるにこそと、心細きままに、栄花なき身に、盛者必衰も知られ、又妻子珍宝もこの世、後の世の侶（とも）にあらずと聞きしかば、心強くも思ひなりて、さても果つべきならば、あらまほしくて、構えて三蜜の法水を汲みて、鎮めに五智の頂に灌べしとて、一人の子をば真言修行の霊場を尋ねて、遣はし置きぬ。然る程に憂かりし年（歳）は暮れて、新玉の春にも成りぬれば、いよいよ風も折知り、浪も時ありて、治まれる　御代は行く末久しく、栄えゆる国の、すめる恨みを、一人残すべきにあらねば、身づから（自ら）鳥の跡を告げつつ、微かに思ふ心を述ぶと雖（いえど）も、我道の業なれば、真の有様を後策（素　こうそ）に著はして、同洩らし申すなるべし。
desc: 絵師は、もとの地のかわりに、都に近い小さな小屋に住まわせてほしいと願います。詞書は、長く待たされるうちに希望が失われ、「盛者必衰」を悟り、妻子や財宝への執着を断ち、真言修行の霊場へ子を送る決意へと進みます。最後には、自分の芸道の真実を後世に残したいという、絵師としての矜持が述べられます。絵巻は、愁訴の物語を追いながらも、絵師の芸術への執念と、出家という結末への静かな諦念を描き出します。
gendaibunen: He asked instead for only a small hut nearer the capital, but the reply dragged on into mid-spring. Sensing that the prosperous must decline, he cut his attachment to wife and child, and sent his son to a Shingon practice site. Even after the new year, he closes his petition wishing to set down the true state of his craft for posterity.
kobunen: "If it is the same either way, please exchange it for a small hut a little nearer," he said, listing many suitable places and submitting them. He was told only that the matter would be considered. From late autumn past until spring was already half gone, his tears of sorrow seemed to deepen; he felt he was sinking utterly. In his frail state he knew that the prosperous must decline, and hearing that wife, children, and treasures are companions neither in this world nor the next, he steeled himself: if this must be the end, he would draw the Dharma-water of the Three Mysteries and pour it upon the crown of the Five Wisdoms for calm—and he sent his only child to seek a sacred site of Shingon practice. As the bitter year ended and a new spring came, wind and waves knew their season; in a peaceful reign that should last long, and a flourishing land, one person ought not remain with lingering resentment. Though he leaves bird-tracks of writing and faintly states his thoughts, because this is the work of his Way, he will set the true state of affairs down for later ages and make it known.
descen: The painter asks, instead of the distant fief, for only a small hut near the capital. As the caption unfolds, hope fades: he perceives the transience of all glory, cuts his attachments to family and possessions, and sends his son to a mountain retreat for Shingon practice. In the end he voices a craftsman's pride—a wish to leave the truth of his art to posterity. The scroll thus traces not only the story of a petition but also the painter's devotion to his art and his quiet resignation toward an ending in monastic life.
